Q: Find a deleted number from a list A:

Why not to use set?

>>> arr = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]
>>> mixed_arr = [1,9,7,4,6,2,3,8]
>>> list(set(arr) - set(mixed_arr))
[5]

This general solution will handle arrays with no constraints on integers, or on the size of lists (or the size of the difference).

In your (very) specific case with positive integers, and only one missing in the other array, it's much more efficient to use the solution from comments below:

>>> abs(sum(arr) - sum(mixed_arr))
5

Q: CSP violation when using Google Fonts A:

Your CSP explicitly allows https://fonts.googleapis.com, but the error shows the stylesheet is being loaded over http://. That protocol mismatch is why it’s blocked.

Make sure the <link> or @import in your page uses https://:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Open+Sans:400,700">

I’d also add a font-src directive for the actual font files - they’re served from fonts.gstatic.com and will be blocked next once the CSS loads. A corrected CSP header in .htaccess would look like:

Header always set Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; style-src-elem 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://fonts.googleapis.com; font-src 'self' https://fonts.gstatic.com"

The font-src directive covers the font binaries that Google Fonts’ CSS then fetches.

Q: HTML file open dialog to access server file system A:

You can do it with ASP.Net... all you need is file system permissions and a simple file browser in a web page, and you can also rename files using the System.IO namespace. Through ASP.Net you can read and modify files on the server. But using JavaScript you will have limited access.

Q: How to `git push` to a repository with different owner on a multi-user system without executing any code from destination? A:

EDIT: In order to ensure this:

answers the question directly, and doesn't wander around in unrelated areas

I have intentionally included quotes, unfortunately, some readers may feel that the quotes still:

wander around in unrelated areas

and by extension, so does this answer (wander around those said areas); sometimes questions just work that way :shug:.

EDIT As the initial question as I encountered it was revised, I have included annotations like this to help emphasis that area is because of a new detail provided by OP's revisions (or quoted comments).

0. Just in case you really don't want any code from the destination repository:

It's not an oversimplification. I would just like to not execute any code from the destination repository. Question is: how?

  1. Intentionally do no action with git push. (e.g., abstinence)

  2. If you do need to submit changes, try git format-patch (from your own trusted copy where you git commit-ed your changes (that you would have wanted to git push))

  3. send the resulting patch to the owner of the repo.

This workflow lets you avoid needing to run non-filesystem operations via git push

1. I'll address the part of CVE-2022-24765 first.

The issue that caused this check was CVE-2022-24765, explained on GitHub's blog here: https://github.blog/open-source/git/git-security-vulnerability-announced/

This is not so much about git as it is about git.exe for windows as explained in CVE-2022-24765:

Git for Windows is a fork of Git containing Windows-specific patches. This vulnerability affects users working on multi-user machines, where untrusted parties have write access to the same hard disk.

2. So Regarding the question phrasing:

On a multi-user Linux system, I would like to push to a non-bare git repository owed by the other user (I have write permission there)

EDIT I originally misunderstood your question as asking about real vulnerabilities on the local system from a distinct local user. As you have clearified in subsequent comments:

I'd just like not execute code from a remote I'm not the owner of.

answer as phrased: Then there is NO relation to CVE-2022-24765 nor its suggested mitigations. Full stop.

EDIT: This is explained well by @jthill in their answer and especially well phrased in their comment

Directly regarding what 'marking as safe' is about...

Git dutifully requires me to mark the directory as safe first

This is to prevent git from loading the config of a repository the invoking user (e.g., your user) does not own on the local filesystem.

See git config safe.directory for more details.

and to avoid wandering we'll skip over the closely related intentionally shared repositories because you did mention this was non-bare (e.g., past the git init step):

a non-bare git repository owed by the other user

Also to to avoid wandering I'll mention git config core.sharedRepository for a config fix of intentionally shared non-bare repositories.

3. Regarding prevention of core.fsmonitor (e.g., local settings on multi-user systems)

as the push could trigger executing arbitrary code (core.fsmonitor, hooks)

Hooks are covered in a different (but similar) question: Skip githooks on git push

EDIT:

As you noted already in the comments:

Whatever is stored in the core.fsmonitor configuration variable also executes and it is not a hook.

(caveat: when you own the repo or have marked the repo as safe)

Regarding core.fsmonitor, this is a local part of git, so I'll explain how they could be used even without hooks (as was asked in over in the afore mentioned question already.), so please bare with me.

Demo of actual risk:

UNTRUSTED_REPO=/tmp/untrusted_repo
mkdir "${UNTRUSTED_REPO}"
cd "${UNTRUSTED_REPO}"
git init
cat > fake-fsmonitor-helper.sh <<'SH'
#! /bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Real fsmonitor helpers speak a protocol;
# but for this demo we will ASSUME a newer version of git protocol to keep it simple

# E.g., in git 2.50 argv[1] is the token Git passes (e.g., a numeric last update token)
TOKEN="${1:-}"  ## git should pass 2 arguments the second should be a token. Demo just store

# and for the demo just ignore it.
unset TOKEN 2>/dev/null || true

# DEMO our 'bad' code
echo "Bad code could/would run here: (demo only)" >&2

# For a safe demo we return an empty set for any request.
#
# We still need to respond to git so: a single line "0" means "no updates".
echo "0"

# and to close the demo just exit
exit 0
SH

# setup our demo code to be excutable
chmod +x fake-fsmonitor-helper.sh

# to make this a remote demo:
# git add fake-fsmonitor-helper.sh
# git commit -m "fake demo fsmonitor"
# git remote add ...
# git push ...
# then others who clone the repo can continue from here
# (skip for simple DEMO ONLY)

# arm our demo code in git config (demo use --worktree to limit scope)
git config --worktree core.fsmonitor "$(pwd)/fake-fsmonitor-helper.sh"

you now have a mostly empty git repo demo that actually does something with fsmonitor

It can be triggered even before a git push, almost by any useful git command really (and of-course not just by other users on a multi-user system, the owner too):

# later trigger untrusted code
$ git status
Bad code could/would run here: (demo only)
On branch master

No commits yet

Bad code could/would run here: (demo only)
Bad code could/would run here: (demo only)
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    fake-fsmonitor-helper.sh

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

(results may differ, e.g., in remotes the fake-fsmonitor-helper.sh would have been already committed, but this a silly demo, and hopefully you get the idea already)

EDIT Namely:

  • This is an edge-case (one, where you should have a serious talk to the other user about their repo's config) where just 'marking the repo as safe' is not a fix.

If this is not what you are asking about, please see https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example and provide an example of your problem.

possible workaround (as I originally answered)

UNTRUSTED_REPO="/Users/Shared/untrusted/repo"
mkdir -p -m 700 "/trusted/jail/"
cp -vf "${UNTRUSTED_REPO}/.git" "/trusted/jail/repo/.git"
rm -vf "/trusted/jail/repo/.git/hooks/*"
# placeholder to use sed/awk to extract only the remote.*.*url config (without running it)
# but that breaks filters and stuff so let's just simplify to:
cat </trusted/jail/repo/.git/config | grep -vF "fsmonitor" 2>/dev/null >> /trusted/jail/repo/.git/config.stripped
mv -vf /trusted/jail/repo/.git/config.stripped /trusted/jail/repo/.git/config
rm -vf "/trusted/jail/repo/.git/info/*"
# enter psudo-jail
printf "%s/n" "Now entering untrusted repo"
cd /trusted/jail/repo/
# spawn a sub-shell perhaps with limmited permissions
bash -r 
# remember
# git config user.email=myemail@example.com
# git config user.name=myself
# start with something like: git checkout --force some-sha (exact place I expect, rather than a branch, just incase I have to git reset --hard)
# cp -vf path/to/my/version/ ./
# make the changes I really need to (because without hooks and info and full config we migh break things)
# git add -p
# git commit
# eventually some kind of hard-core push (perhaps without ever doing fetch)
# git push --no-prune --atomic --force
# exit
wait ; # but eventually exit sub-shell
# clean up
cd "${OLDPWD:-$HOME}"
# rm -vfrd /trusted/jail/repo/*

EDIT To explain a bit more: the key peice here is to remove the dangerous config E.g.:

cat </trusted/jail/repo/.git/config | grep -vF "fsmonitor" 2>/dev/null >> /trusted/jail/repo/.git/config.stripped
mv -vf /trusted/jail/repo/.git/config.stripped /trusted/jail/repo/.git/config

To keep this answer short as possible, I've intentionally ignored similar issues with git filters or hooks (albeit we removed the default hooks directory in this example workaround)

Dispite the simplicity of the mitigations here, the idea is generalizable to:

  • sandbox the git directory
  • prune hooks and info (info just makes it too complex here with sparse checkouts and stuff)
  • sanitize the config (in practice you'll probably only want to keep the remote.url & remote.pushurl & remote.fetch (e.g., the values for the remote), and patch with your own "trusted" default settings instead, but this demo is kept simple here)
  • once the config and hooks are sanitized, you'll have to open the repo if you want to use git, so git checkout and do stuff (e.g., overwrite something with a company asset, etc.)
  • finally you are ready to git push the changes (where your question is centered)
  • then all that's left is cleanup (e.g., consider the sandbox ephemeral and toss it, make a new one next time)

4. None of this relates to git remote (the destination of a git push)

Instead, is there any way to push to the remote, but prevent any code defined in it from running?

With the configuration sanitized (or marked safe) this is exactly like a normal git push of a repo your user owns, and is answered already by Skip githooks on git push (how to skip githooks on push)

Relevent Refs:

  • NVD CVE-2022-24765
  • OP's link to GitHUb Blog on the CVE-2022-24765
  • The Book of Git

Q: What is the difference between .cfg and .conf in linux? A:

The difference is the spelling. That's it.

There's no particular significance in the different spellings. Both are short for "configuration". There's no real standard for what configuration files should be called. (Or rather, there are too many standards.)

Apparently the authors of some programs preferred .conf, and others preferred .cfg.

If you need to create a configuration file for a particular program, you just have to use the name that program expects.

Q: How to delete file from subfolders in sharepoint using power automate A:

After few research, i found that a http request is very effective and let you specify the file path and the filename. I needed to receive the filename from an email to delete a specific file. In the image above, i only show the filename as text but you would need to a substring action in the email body to get the filename.

As you can see, i used the "Get file metadata using path" where i only did a concat to specify the required file path and filename from compose actions : concat('/',outputs('repertoire'),'/',outputs('fichier')) Finally, the "Send an http request to sharepoint" refer to the following Uri :

_api/web/GetFolderByServerRelativeUrl('Documents partages/Compte-rendu')/Files('outputs('Get_file_metadata_using_path')?['body/DisplayName']')

and the "display name" is selected from the Get file action.

Enjoy !
